items.memoText:
VETO MESSAGE - No. 159
 
TO THE ASSEMBLY:
 
I am returning herewith, without my approval, the following bill:
 
Assembly Bill Number 6371-B, entitled:
 
    "AN ACT to amend the education law, in relation to authorizing phar-
      macists to refill non-controlled substance prescriptions for quan-
      tities  of  drugs  not  to  exceed a ninety day supply, subject to
      certain conditions"
 
    NOT APPROVED
 
  This bill  would  authorize  pharmacists  to  exercise  discretion  in
refilling  non-controlled  drug  prescriptions  up  to  a 90-day supply,
subject to certain conditions.
 
  My administration's  commitment  to  combatting  the  opioid  epidemic
sweeping  across  our  State is unwavering. These efforts include imple-
menting the comprehensive I-STOP law to curb  prescription  drug  abuse,
limiting  initial opioid prescriptions for acute pain from 30 to 7 days,
and requiring on-going education on addiction and  pain  management  for
all  prescribers. Moreover, this year's budget invests over $200 million
to support prevention, treatment, and recovery programs targeted  toward
chemical dependence and education activities.
 
  I  vetoed  a similar version of this bill last year because it did not
further these goals and in many instances, would have actively run coun-
ter to them. (Veto No. 247 of 2016). The 2016 bill would  have  promoted
the  unnecessary  filling of prescription medication, thus leading to an
increase in the amount of unused drugs in  circulation.  It  also  would
have  allowed  pharmacists  to unilaterally determine that an additional
supply of a drug refill is warranted without first obtaining the practi-
tioner's approval.

  To determine if there was a feasible solution to  address  the  public
health and safety concerns raised by this bill, the Department of Health
met  with other impacted agencies, sponsors, and stakeholders. Yet while
I appreciate the Legislature's efforts to modify its proposal,  such  as
requiring  the  pharmacist to notify the patient's physician of a refill
in a more expedited manner and limiting patients to five 90-day  refills
annually,  they  do  not sufficiently mitigate the two concerns I raised
last year.
 
  First, the bill retains the provisions that would risk contributing to
the distribution of larger quantities of  prescription  medication  than
may  be  necessary  for a specific patient. Second, it would still allow
the pharmacist to infringe on the physician-patient relationship.  While
the  pharmacist  must  notify  the physician of a refill in a more expe-
ditious manner, the pharmacist can still make  that  notification  after
the prescription is filled. Thus, pharmacists would be able to unilater-
ally  determine  if  an  additional supply of a drug refill is warranted
without first obtaining the practitioner's approval.
 
  For these reasons, I am again constrained to veto this bill.  However,
I  am  directing  the  Department  of  Health to continue its efforts to
 
collaborate with other interested parties to examine the feasibility  of
a solution that addresses my concerns.
 
  The bill is disapproved.                    (signed) ANDREW M. CUOMO
 
                               __________
